_comment: What this stack's machines must DO, declared by the stack (#503).
The shape and the rules are documented once, in
examples/stacks/scaleway/proof.json. What follows is only what differs on

_why: 80 rather than 443: it is the port outscale_security_group_rule.web_http
opens, the port the balancer's listener carries and the port its health
check names. One port, named three times in main.tf, and until #503 no
machine of this stack listened on any of them.
_closed_port: The public path's closed half (#548), the same shape the Scaleway stack
declares: 80 is opened by outscale_security_group_rule.web_http, 9090 is
named by no rule, both listen on the machine whose PublicIp the station
This cloud is the control population for that change: a Vm is born on its
Subnet, so its public address has ridden a managed NIC since the first
boot and no migration was ever needed here. If this half went red while
Scaleway's passed, the cause would be the assertion and not the remedy.

_why: platform-app sits in another Subnet of the same Net, and 8080 is what
outscale_security_group_rule.app_from_web opens to public-a, where the
restarted machine lives. So the pair crosses the Net's router, which is
the path #549 measured a restart losing on the other cloud.
control is a skip and not a machine, for the same reason platform-web-b
is the firewall family's control_source here: the rule names
10.50.1.0/24 alone, so web-b is refused on 8080 by design, and a machine
that must be refused cannot be the control of a reachability pass.

control.skip: no second machine of this stack reaches platform-app on 8080: outscale_security_group_rule.app_from_web names 10.50.1.0/24, and platform-web-b sits in public-b, which is exactly why it serves as the firewall family's control_source. An unrestarted machine the rule refuses would prove nothing about a restart, so the before-probe of the restarted machine carries the pass alone here. The Scaleway stack's platform-web-1 is the neighbour control.

_why: outscale_security_group_rule.app_from_web opens 8080 to 10.50.1.0/24,
which is public-a, where platform-web-a lives. 9090 is named by no rule.
Both probes leave platform-web-a and both cross the Net's router, so the
receiver's policy is what decides.
control_source is the second negative control, and it is the one the
Scaleway stack cannot offer: platform-web-b sits in public-b, a block the
rule does not name, so its 8080 must be refused where platform-web-a's is
not. Same port, same target, two sources: the only difference between the
two verdicts is whose address the rule names. Measured 2026-08-27, both
halves. Liveness is proved separately, from inside the target, before any
refusal is read as a firewall verdict.

reaches._why: Two subnets of one Net, on the port their shared group opens to 0.0.0.0/0. A Net that routes between its own subnets is what upstream does and what the peering resources below it assume.

isolated.skip: this stack declares no unpeered pair with a machine on each side: outscale_net_peering joins the workload and services Nets on purpose, and the services Net carries an interface (outscale_nic.app_services) rather than a machine of its own. The cross-VPC separation is asserted by the Scaleway stack and by tools/conformance/outscale/network.sh, which builds two unpeered Nets for exactly this.

_why: The stack's balancer spans two subnets on purpose (the ztiac shape that
found #457 then #483), and under OVN the runtime distributes only to
backends of the balancer's own subnet. So this declaration does not name
an expected backend count: the harness reads the pack's own delivery
record (`balancer-distributed` / `balancer-undistributed` in Runtime),
requires every reply to name a distributed backend, requires no reply
ever to name a withheld one, and says how many were distributed. It
therefore strengthens by itself the day the bound moves, instead of
carrying a number that would then be wrong.
client is the machine the probes leave, and it must sit in the balancer's
own subnet: the public face of an internet-facing balancer answers for
two minutes and goes dark (#315), so asserting it would assert a defect.
balancer.name: platform-front

_why: Measured on 2026-08-27 by reading what every machine of this stack
carries. See the Scaleway stack's declaration for why this is asserted
after the restarts and what a moved number means.
